known: Default provider is SQLite with a hard-coded local file connection string (src/Conduit/Program.cs:15-16).
No indexes are declared in the EF model (src/Conduit/Infrastructure/ConduitContext.cs).
Schema created by EnsureCreated at startup (src/Conduit/Program.cs:120-124).
Article list default page size is 20 (src/Conduit/Features/Articles/List.cs:125).
assumed: Tables grow beyond tens of thousands of rows in production - affects PERF-001, PERF-002
Heavy-tailed favorites, comments and follows per entity - affects PERF-002, PERF-003, PERF-004
derived: Joined rows per article = favorites x tags (EF single query over two collection Includes) - from ArticleExtensions.cs:9-14

decision_changing_questions.question: Approximate row counts of Articles and Persons in production, and which database provider is used?
decision_changing_questions.what_it_would_change: Whether PERF-001/002 are High P1 or negligible.

decision_changing_questions.question: Typical and maximum favorites, tags, comments and follows per entity?

root_causes.description: No indexes on the columns every request filters by (Article.Slug, Person.Username, Person.Email, Article.CreatedAt)
Article list/detail load Author + Favorites + Tags as joined collections (row multiplication) and fetch the full Body that list responses discard
Whole follow lists are loaded into memory to answer a single membership check
Comment endpoints load and track every comment of an article, unbounded; create/delete load them just to modify one
Article list issues a second, synchronous COUNT query on the request thread
Every request, including pure reads, opens a synchronous ReadCommitted transaction
Article create does per-tag FindAsync/SaveChanges and a slug-uniqueness probe loop with one query per collision
Serilog is configured at Verbose to a synchronous console sink and there are no metrics or traces

findings.problem: The EF model declares no index on the lookup columns used by nearly every endpoint, so those lookups are table scans that grow with row count.
findings.performance_principle: Selective lookups should cost proportional to the result size, not the table size; access paths must exist for the predicates and sort orders the hot paths use.

evidence.statement: OnModelCreating configures only composite keys/FKs for ArticleTag, ArticleFavorite, FollowedPeople and DateTime conversions; no HasIndex anywhere.
grep for HasIndex/[Index] across src/Conduit returns nothing; Slug and Username/Email are plain string properties.
Slug equality lookup is the entry of Details, Edit, Delete, Favorites, Comments list/create/delete (e.g. Details.cs:43-45, Comments/Create.cs:36-38).
Username equality lookup runs for the current user on feed, create, favorite, profile paths (e.g. Articles/Create.cs:42-45); Email lookup on every login and registration.
Article list orders by CreatedAt DESC, ArticleId DESC with Skip/Take and no index on CreatedAt.
Schema is created by EnsureCreated at startup; no migrations that could add indexes elsewhere.
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters once Articles/Persons tables are large enough that a scan is not cheap; no table-size or traffic figure is supplied, so assumed: tables grow beyond tens of thousands of rows in production. Negligible for small demo datasets.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for HasIndex, [Index], unique constraints, and migrations; none found.
Table sizes are unknown and the shipped default is a local SQLite file, so scan cost may be negligible in practice; this caps confidence at Medium.

findings.recommendation: Add indexes (unique where the domain demands: Person.Username, Person.Email, Article.Slug) and an index on Article(CreatedAt, ArticleId) via OnModelCreating, so lookups and the list ordering use an access path. Unique indexes also close the check-then-insert race (see COR-001).
findings.trade_offs: Extra write cost and storage per insert; EnsureCreated will not alter an existing database, so existing deployments need a manual migration/script. Unique indexes can fail to apply if duplicates already exist.

validation.metric: Query plan for SELECT by Slug / Username / Email and for the article-list ORDER BY; rows examined
validation.expectation: Plans change from table scan to index seek; rows examined per lookup drops from table size to about 1.
validation.falsifier: Plans already show index use, or lookups on production-sized data are already sub-millisecond.
validation.guard: A test or migration check asserting the indexes exist.

commands.command: sqlite3 realworld.db "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM Articles WHERE Slug='x';"
commands.purpose: Show whether the Slug lookup scans the table (run against a copy of the data).

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If the deployment is a demo/benchmark with a few hundred rows, scans on SQLite are microseconds and nothing here is observable.

alternatives.why: Removes the scan at the source and enforces uniqueness at no extra request cost.
Adds invalidation complexity and does not fix the list sort.

findings.problem: GetAllData includes two collection navigations (ArticleFavorites, ArticleTags) in one query, so each article returns favorites x tags joined rows; the list handler also loads every article body only to set it to null.
findings.performance_principle: Fetch only the data the response needs, and avoid joining independent one-to-many relations in one result set, which multiplies rows instead of adding them.

evidence.statement: GetAllData includes Author, ArticleFavorites and ArticleTags with no AsSplitQuery.
List handler uses GetAllData, then sets article.Body = null for every row after materialisation.
Favorites are fetched as full rows only so Favorited/FavoritesCount can use List.Count.
Derivation: rows per article returned by the join = max(1,favorites) x max(1,tags); e.g. an article with 3 tags and 50 favorites yields 150 rows (illustrative inputs, not measured).
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters for the main list/feed endpoints when popular articles accumulate many favorites and several tags and the page size is the caller-supplied Limit (default 20). Assumed workload is read-heavy list traffic; unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for AsSplitQuery/QuerySplittingBehavior configuration or projections; none found (UseSqlite(connectionString) without options).
Page is capped per request by Take(Limit ?? 20), but Limit has no upper bound in the handler.

findings.recommendation: Project to a response DTO in SQL (author fields, tag names, favorites count via correlated count, favorited flag via Any, no Body for list) instead of materialising entities with Includes; if entities are kept, use AsSplitQuery. Clamp Limit.
findings.trade_offs: DTO projection duplicates part of the Article JSON shape and changes serialization wiring; split query adds round trips.

validation.metric: Rows returned and bytes transferred by the GET /api/articles query; EF Core logged SQL
validation.expectation: Rows per page drop to the page size (<= Limit) and Body bytes disappear from list queries.
validation.falsifier: Measured row count per page already equals page size on representative data.
validation.guard: An integration test asserting query shape/row count for the list endpoint.

commands.purpose: Run existing article tests as a functional baseline before changing the query.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: With small favorite/tag counts per article the product is tiny and EF's page subquery keeps it bounded; the Body column is usually modest in size.

alternatives.option: Select-projection with counts computed in the database
alternatives.why: Removes both the row multiplication and unused columns.
Removes the cartesian product but still transfers full favorite rows and Body.
Hides cost, adds invalidation on favorite/edit.

findings.problem: ProfileReader loads the current user with both Following and Followers collections tracked, then calls Any on one of them; the feed path loads all Followers rows too and passes them to a Contains subquery.
findings.performance_principle: Membership questions should be answered by the datastore with a keyed existence check, not by materialising a whole relationship.

evidence.statement: Persons.Include(Following).Include(Followers) for the current user, then currentPerson.Followers.Any(TargetId == ...); Following is never read.
Feed: Persons.Include(Followers) is materialised, then a Contains over its TargetIds is embedded in the article query.
The same two Includes also create a followers x following row product in one query.
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters for users with large follow lists hitting profile and feed endpoints; follow-count distribution unknown, assumed to have a heavy tail.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for a follow-count limit; none exists in Followers/Add.cs.
Average users likely follow few people, bounding typical cost.

findings.recommendation: Replace with FollowedPeople.AnyAsync(f => f.Observer.Username == name && f.TargetId == id) and, for the feed, express the follow set as a subquery in SQL rather than loading it.
findings.trade_offs: Slightly more verbose queries; none otherwise.

validation.metric: Rows read per GET /api/profiles/{u} and feed request
validation.expectation: Rows drop from follow-list size to 1.
validation.falsifier: Follow lists in production are uniformly tiny.
validation.guard: Test with a user following many accounts asserting bounded queries.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: For typical accounts the loaded lists are small and the request is dominated by other work.

findings.problem: Comments list has no paging and is tracked, and Comments/Create and Delete load the article's full Comments collection to add or remove a single comment.
findings.performance_principle: Per-request work and memory must be bounded by what the caller needs, not by the total size of a growing collection.

evidence.statement: List: Articles.Include(Comments).ThenInclude(Author) with no limit or AsNoTracking.
Create: Articles.Include(Comments) then article.Comments.Add(comment).
Delete: Articles.Include(Comments).ThenInclude(Author).
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters on articles with large comment threads (hot articles); the RealWorld API returns all comments, so listing cannot be fully bounded without a contract change. Thread sizes unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: The API contract returns the full comment list, which bounds how much list can be reduced.
No comment cap or paging found.

findings.recommendation: Make list AsNoTracking with a projection; in Create/Delete query the article id (AnyAsync/Select) and add or delete the comment by key without loading the collection.
findings.trade_offs: Slightly different EF patterns; list still returns all comments.

validation.metric: Rows loaded and allocations for POST /api/articles/{slug}/comments on an article with many comments
validation.expectation: Write cost becomes independent of existing comment count.
validation.guard: Test creating a comment on an article with many comments, asserting query count/rows.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Typical article comment counts are small; only list is constrained by the API contract.

alternatives.why: Removes load of unrelated comments on writes.
Breaks the expected response shape unless negotiated.

findings.problem: queryable.Count() is the sync API called inside an async handler, blocking a thread-pool thread for the duration of a second round trip.
findings.performance_principle: Do not block threads on I/O in an async path; blocked threads reduce capacity under concurrency.

evidence.statement: ArticlesCount = queryable.Count() after the awaited page query.
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters only under high concurrency on a networked database (SQL Server); with local SQLite the I/O is in-process anyway. The count also scans because filters are unindexed (PERF-001).

counter_evidence.statement: Default provider is in-process SQLite where blocking is cheap.

validation.metric: Thread-pool queue length / request latency under concurrent list load
validation.expectation: No blocked threads on the count call.
validation.falsifier: Thread pool never saturates under target load.

findings.problem: The mediator pipeline wraps every handler in BeginTransaction/Commit, using the synchronous Database.BeginTransaction.
findings.performance_principle: Hold connections and locks only for work that needs them; avoid blocking calls on async paths.

evidence.statement: DBContextTransactionPipelineBehavior calls context.BeginTransaction()/CommitTransaction() for all requests.
BeginTransaction uses sync Database.BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted).
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters mainly with SQLite writers (single-writer lock) or a small SQL Server pool under high concurrency; unmeasured and assumed small otherwise.

counter_evidence.statement: Transaction ends with the handler, so hold time equals handler time; per-request O(1) overhead only.

findings.recommendation: Skip the transaction for query handlers (e.g. via a marker interface) and keep it for commands.
findings.trade_offs: Reads lose transactional grouping across multiple statements in one handler.

validation.metric: Connection hold time and DB lock wait for read endpoints
validation.falsifier: No measurable difference at target concurrency.

findings.problem: Each new tag is saved immediately in a loop (one round trip per tag, plus FindAsync each), and the slug loop issues one AnyAsync per suffix attempt.
findings.performance_principle: Batch round trips instead of paying one per item.

evidence.statement: foreach tag: FindAsync, then AddAsync + SaveChangesAsync inside the loop.
for-loop AnyAsync(Slug == uniqueSlug) increments the suffix until free; same pattern in Edit.cs.
No runtime evidence exists in the repository (no benchmarks, query plans, traces, or metrics).

findings.conditions: Matters for creates with many new tags or many same-titled articles (slug probes grow with number of collisions); expected to be small per request.

counter_evidence.statement: Tag list per article is typically a handful; slug collisions require identical titles.

findings.recommendation: Load all existing tags with one Contains query and add new Tag rows in one SaveChanges; fetch existing slugs with StartsWith(slug) once and pick the next suffix in memory.
findings.trade_offs: Race window on concurrent same-title/tag creates needs the unique indexes from PERF-001.

validation.metric: Statement count for POST /api/articles with N new tags

findings.problem: MinimumLevel.Verbose with a console sink may emit every EF Core SQL statement per request synchronously; no metrics, tracing or benchmarks exist to measure any other finding.
findings.performance_principle: Instrumentation overhead should be bounded and the system must be measurable.

evidence.statement: MinimumLevel.Verbose() and WriteTo.Console, commented 'just for local debug', but unconditional.
No OpenTelemetry, metrics or load-test artifacts found in the repository.
No logging configuration file exists (no appsettings*.json), so framework filters are unverified.

findings.conditions: Matters if the effective level lets EF command logging through at Information/Debug in production; whether it does depends on logging filters not visible in the repo.

counter_evidence.statement: Microsoft logging filter defaults may suppress Debug/Verbose categories before reaching Serilog; unverified.

findings.recommendation: Make level and sink configuration-driven (Information or above in production); add basic request metrics/tracing so the other findings can be validated.

validation.metric: Log lines per request and console write time
validation.falsifier: Effective level already Warning+ in deployment.

considered_not_reported.observation: Password hashing (single HMAC pass) is cheap, so login is not a CPU bottleneck; it is a security weakness instead (SEC-001).
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Cheap and bounded per login; no performance impact.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: The hash is replaced with a proper KDF.

considered_not_reported.observation: SQLite single-writer locking as default provider.
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Provider is a hard-coded local default; no evidence of production use or write concurrency.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Production provider and write rate are known.

adjacent_findings.problem: Passwords are hashed with a single HMAC-SHA512 pass keyed with the hard-coded string 'realworld' and a per-user salt; the JWT signing key is also a hard-coded literal. Hash comparison uses SequenceEqual (not constant time).

evidence.statement: HMACSHA512 constructed from a literal key; single ComputeHashAsync, no iterations or memory-hard KDF.
Signing key is a literal in source.
Login compares hashes with SequenceEqual.

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Use a standard password hashing API (PBKDF2/Argon2/bcrypt via ASP.NET Identity's hasher), load the JWT key from secret configuration, and compare in constant time. The cheap hash is also why login is not a CPU hotspot; a proper KDF will make login CPU-heavy by design and should be capacity-tested.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A dedicated security review / threat model; dependency and secrets scanning.

adjacent_findings.problem: Username, email and slug uniqueness is enforced only by check-then-insert queries with no unique constraint, so concurrent requests can create duplicates.

evidence.statement: Registration checks Any(Username) and Any(Email) then inserts.
No unique indexes in the model.

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Add unique indexes (see PERF-001) and handle the constraint violation as a 409.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: Concurrency-focused correctness tests against a real database.
